findings.title: Direction and subdued sound as one course of attention
findings.claim: The command about walking gives movement a direction, while the command about voice reduces its audible force. In 20:108, following the Caller without deviation meets voices reduced to whisper; read together, the focus's two commands can describe a coordinated way of moving and attending, with quiet making room for hearing.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries direction through ٱقْصِدْ in the domain of walking and carries reduction through ٱغْضُضْ مِن صَوْتِكَ. The supplied 20:108 scene joins following without deviation to hearing only a whisper, so direction and lowered sound contact as an attentive course rather than two unrelated style rules. The wide reader-walk note also places the commands after public counsel and a warning against exultant gait, but that context remains attributed.
findings.reader_payoff: A reader can see the gait and voice commands as one disciplined orientation toward a call, and can hear lowering as creating room for attention as well as regulating volume.
findings.containment: The focus remains a direct instruction about walking and voice. The Day-of-Calling scene is an analogy, not an assertion that the focus describes that scene or predicts an eschatological state. The 31:17–18 link is legacy reader-walk evidence without exact Arabic in this packet.

findings.mechanism: The focus repeats the sound-domain, ranks the donkey's sound as most objectionable, and ends with the animal as its literal source. In 31:6, voiced talk diverts from guidance; in 31:7, pride appears as turning away as though one had not heard. These independent context cues meet the focus's NKR and sound carriers, allowing objectionability to include failed social recognition alongside harshness.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish a sound that reaches the ear from speech that is received as meaningful address; the donkey comparison remains audible while its communicative edge becomes visible.
findings.containment: The ordinary comparison remains the donkey's sound, and the local acoustic reading remains live. The contextual inference concerns the human social effect of forceful speech; it does not attribute communicative intent to the donkey or claim that the sound is physically inaudible.
